title: UNION
description: Combine compatible row sets, retain the intended identity and NULL semantics, and distinguish full-row deduplication from source provenance and final ordering.

questions.question_text: What does UNION do?
options: Returns rows common to two queries
Combines the rows of two queries, keeping the distinct set from either
Returns rows in the first query but not the second
Joins two tables on a shared column
questions.explanation: UNION merges two result sets, removing duplicates.

questions.question_text: In the running example, does UNION include student 2 (enrolled in both years) once or twice?
options: Twice
Once — UNION removes duplicate rows automatically
Zero times
This depends on ORDER BY
questions.explanation: Automatic de-duplication means a student present in both source queries appears only once.

questions.question_text: Which ORDER BY establishes the final combined UNION result order?
options: Any branch order automatically becomes the final order
The ORDER BY on the combined result; parenthesized local branch selection can have separate engine-specific ordering
Only a physical primary key
No UNION query can be ordered
questions.explanation: A branch can use local ordering for selection under supported syntax, but only the final ordering establishes the combined output sequence.

questions.question_text: What must be true of the two queries combined by UNION?
options: They must query the same table
They must return the same number of columns with compatible types
They must both include an ORDER BY
They must both return at least 10 rows
questions.explanation: Union-compatibility (matching column count/types) is a hard requirement, checked before deduplication.

questions.question_text: What is the performance implication of UNION's automatic de-duplication?
options: It has no performance cost
It has a real computational cost — comparing rows to remove duplicates — that UNION ALL avoids
De-duplication is always instantaneous regardless of data size
It only costs time on the second query, never the first
questions.explanation: De-duplication requires real comparison work, motivating UNION ALL when duplicates aren't a concern.

questions.question_text: If enrolled_2025 has 4 students and enrolled_2026 has 3, with 2 students in both, how many rows does UNION return?
questions.explanation: For distinct source identity sets of sizes4 and3 with2 identities shared, the union has4+3-2=5 distinct students. Raw row counts with internal duplicates need separate treatment.

questions.question_text: Is UNION a relational-algebra concept, a SQL-specific feature, or both?
options: A SQL-only feature with no theoretical basis
Both — Union is a foundational relational algebra operation (7.4), and SQL's UNION keyword implements it directly
A relational-algebra-only concept with no SQL equivalent
Exclusive to NoSQL query languages
questions.explanation: This chapter revisits the SQL syntax for a concept already introduced theoretically in Chapter 7.

questions.question_text: Can more than two queries be combined with UNION in a single statement?
options: No, exactly two queries maximum
Yes — any number of SELECT queries can be chained with UNION between each pair
Only three queries maximum
Only if they all query the same table
questions.explanation: Several compatible query blocks can be chained, subject to the engine’s practical limits and the expression’s grouping/duplicate rules; not a literally unlimited resource guarantee.

questions.question_text: What columns determine duplicate elimination in UNION?
options: The complete projected row
Only the first source primary key automatically
Only the last alias
Only numeric columns
questions.explanation: Distinctness uses the output row rather than an unseen business identifier.

questions.question_text: A student appears in two years and year is selected. Must UNION collapse both rows?
options: Yes, student_id always dominates
No, the year values can make the full rows distinct
Only if ordered
Only after a join
questions.explanation: Projection changes the fact identity being deduplicated.

questions.question_text: Does matching alias text reorder mismatched column positions?
options: Yes, automatically
No
Only for strings
Only when one source is empty
questions.explanation: Set operators align selected columns positionally.

questions.question_text: Does UNION guarantee sorted output without ORDER BY?
options: Yes, distinct always means sorted
Only for integer identifiers
No
Only with two sources
questions.explanation: Distinctness and output ordering are separate contracts.

questions.question_text: Can duplicate identifiers inside one input be removed by UNION?
options: No, only cross-source overlaps are removed
Only if indexed
Only when aliases match
Yes
questions.explanation: The combined distinct result removes equal projected rows from any source.

questions.question_text: What does adding a source label change?
options: It can make otherwise equal projected rows distinct
It never changes duplicate semantics
It automatically authenticates the source
It removes all NULLs
questions.explanation: The label becomes part of the compared output row.

questions.question_text: Can equal NULL positions be deduplicated in a set result?
options: No, NULL rows are always unique
Yes
Only without SELECT
Only for a text key
questions.explanation: Set duplicate comparison differs from ordinary NULL equality predicates.

questions.question_text: What can a case-insensitive collation affect?
options: Only the query font
Only the number of tables
Whether textual rows compare equal for deduplication
Whether UNION is legal at all
questions.explanation: Comparison rules belong to the result type and collation contract.

questions.question_text: Why might institution_id need to accompany student_id?
options: It always doubles performance
It replaces every permission check
It forces all rows to match
Student numbers can be local to an institution
questions.explanation: Cross-source identity must be scoped to the real domain.

questions.question_text: Does local branch ordering guarantee final combined order?
options: No
Yes, in every engine
Only if the alias is short
Only with one column
questions.explanation: Final ordering is a separate outer contract.

questions.question_text: Can a later ALL restore duplicates already removed by an earlier distinct step?
options: Yes, always
No
Only after ORDER BY
Only with three tables
questions.explanation: Grouping and duplicate scope must be analyzed across the expression.

questions.question_text: What is necessary before replacing UNION with UNION ALL?
options: Only a shorter query
Only a row-count screenshot
A requirement that the resulting multiplicity is correct
Only a new index
questions.explanation: Performance work must preserve the intended population and duplicate policy.

coding_problems.title: Combine distinct student-club memberships
coding_problems.task: Return distinct student_id, club_id pairs appearing in either membership table. A student in two clubs has two result rows. Order by student_id, club_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE memberships_a(student_id INT NOT NULL,club_id INT NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE memberships_b(student_id INT NOT NULL,club_id INT NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO memberships_a VALUES(1,10),(1,20),(2,10),(2,10); INSERT INTO memberships_b VALUES(1,10),(3,30);
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT student_id,club_id FROM memberships_a UNION SELECT student_id,club_id FROM memberships_b ORDER BY student_id,club_id;
hints: Project both identity components in the same order.
coding_problems.explanation: UNION removes only identical full membership pairs, not every repeated student identifier.

notes:
## Combine compatible row populations and remove duplicate rows

UNION combines the result rows of compatible query blocks and removes duplicate result rows. It is useful when several sources represent the same kind of fact, such as student identifiers enrolled in different years. Unlike a join, it stacks compatible row populations rather than pairing related columns side by side. Define the output columns and identity before deciding whether duplicate elimination is required.

UNION ALL retains all contributed rows instead. The distinction is a result contract, not merely a performance preference. If the question asks for distinct students ever enrolled, UNION can express that set. If it asks for every enrollment event, discarding equal projections can erase legitimate events. A faster query answering a different question is not an optimization of the original requirement.

## Follow the retained two-year enrollment exercise

The first source contains student identifiers 1, 2, 3 and 4. The second contains 2, 3 and 5. The distinct union is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Students 2 and 3 appear once even though they occur in both years. Repeated identifiers within one source are also eliminated from the final distinct result, so the duplicate policy applies to the combined result rather than only overlaps between tables.

```sql
SELECT student_id FROM enrolled_2025
UNION
SELECT student_id FROM enrolled_2026
ORDER BY student_id;
```

Both source columns are declared NOT NULL in the retained exercise. The result is sorted because the final ORDER BY explicitly requires that order. UNION's duplicate elimination does not by itself create a contractual sorted result. A different plan or engine can implement distinctness without returning rows in the sequence a small fixture happened to display.

If the first source has four distinct identifiers and the second has three, with two distinct identifiers shared, the union has five. The subtraction formula relies on counts of sets at the same identity grain. Raw row counts with within-source duplicates do not satisfy that assumption. Compute the intended distinct identities before using a quick cardinality formula.

## Align columns by position and compatible meaning

Each query block must supply the same number of columns with compatible types under the engine's rules. UNION aligns the first selected column with the first, the second with the second, and so on. Matching aliases do not rearrange the values. A source returning student_id, name must not be stacked with another returning name, student_id merely because both outputs have two columns.

```sql
SELECT person_id,display_name FROM current_participants
UNION
SELECT participant_id AS person_id,participant_name AS display_name
FROM archived_participants;
```

The aliases communicate one shared contract, while the positional projections implement it. Make units and type conversions explicit when they differ. A numeric customer identifier and a text region code should not share a column solely because the engine can coerce both to a common representation. Compatible syntax is weaker than compatible business meaning.

## Understand full-row duplicate elimination

UNION compares the complete projected row. Selecting only student_id deduplicates that identity. Selecting student_id, enrollment_year keeps two rows for a student enrolled in two different years because their year values differ. Adding a source label can similarly make previously equal rows distinct. That is useful provenance when intended, but it changes what duplicate means.

Two different people sharing a display name can collapse into one row if the projection contains only that name. Retain stable identifiers when the report distinguishes people. Conversely, including an event identifier means two events remain separate even if the person and amount match. Choose the projection from the desired fact grain before reasoning about whether UNION removes too much or too little.

## Include NULL and collation in row equality

Set-operation duplicate elimination treats equal projected NULL positions as duplicates under its result comparison semantics, even though ordinary NULL=NULL is UNKNOWN in a predicate. A one-column union of two NULL-producing rows therefore has one distinct NULL row. Do not import a WHERE comparison truth table unchanged into duplicate-elimination reasoning.

Text comparison also follows the result's type and collation rules. Case variants can compare equal under a case-insensitive collation, while a binary comparison can retain them separately. Padding and coercion can affect results too. An original exercise using integer identifiers avoids many of these complications; porting the reasoning to names requires explicit comparison assumptions and representative fixtures.

## Apply filters before and after the combination deliberately

Each query block can filter its own source population. A branch-level WHERE for the specified year or approved status determines which facts are contributed. A filter over a derived combined result applies after the branches have produced their rows. Moving a predicate across a boundary can be valid under suitable conditions, but it must preserve type, missingness and duplicate behavior.

If one source's deleted records are excluded and another's are not, the final report may contain inconsistent eligibility. Document shared rules and source-specific differences explicitly. A cross-system union can also require identity reconciliation: student_id7 from one institution may not identify the same person as student_id7 from another. Add a source namespace when the business identity requires it rather than merging unrelated entities accidentally.

## Keep branch selection separate from final ordering

The final ORDER BY sorts the combined result and uses the output naming rules of the set expression. A branch can sometimes use its own ORDER BY and LIMIT inside required parentheses to select a bounded subset. That local ordering does not guarantee the final union's display order. The exact syntax is engine-specific, so verify it before claiming ORDER BY can appear only once anywhere in a UNION statement.

A top-five-from-each-source report differs from top-five-over-the-combined-population. Applying LIMIT before combination selects local candidates; applying it after a final global order selects from the final result. Include ties and an uneven source distribution to expose that distinction. A test where both sources have one row cannot establish the intended top-N semantics.

## Treat execution cost as a separate question

Distinctness requires comparison work, which can involve hashing, sorting or other engine strategies. It does not imply a guaranteed final sort, one particular temporary structure or a universal latency penalty of a known size. UNION ALL can avoid distinct-result work when its preserved multiplicity is correct, but source access, filters, network transfer and final ordering still contribute cost.

Several UNION and UNION ALL operators in one expression require attention to grouping and duplicate scope. Parentheses and the engine's set-operation precedence rules determine which intermediate populations are distinct or retained. Do not assume a later ALL retroactively restores rows already removed by an earlier distinct operation. State the required whole expression and challenge it with repeated rows from several branches.

## Verify a rewrite through counterexamples

Compare the proposed alternative on overlap, within-source duplicates, an empty branch and two different identities sharing the same label. Verify column positions and output types as well as row counts. Matching counts can hide one lost identity and one extra identity. If the rewrite introduces a source tag or removes an identifier, explain the new comparison grain before interpreting any timing improvement. A reproducible correctness fixture should accompany the query so a later added column does not quietly change which rows are considered duplicates.

Check missingness and duplicate provenance explicitly as separate concerns.

## Solve two compatible-population exercises

The beginner task preserves the original enrolled 2025/enrolled 2026 setup and asks for distinct student identifiers across both sources. Verify the original and alternate fixtures, then add repeated identifiers inside one source and an empty source. The distinct final set should still preserve each required student once, with no invented row for an empty population.

For the intermediate task, combine student and club identifiers from two years. The full pair defines membership identity: one student in two different clubs must produce two rows, while a repeated identical pair across years appears once. Add equal student names only as optional description after the membership identity is established. Continue with [UNION ALL](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/union-all), [set compatibility](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/set-compatibility) and [duplicate handling](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/duplicate-handling) to connect projection, identity and execution cost.
